blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The chi-square (χ²) test compares the observed counts (O) in the categories of a table with the counts expected (E) if a null hypothesis were true. Pearson’s statistic is

X² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E, summed over every cell.

Under H₀, and when expected counts are not too small (§10.6.1), X² approximately follows a χ² distribution (recall §5.7.2.4), whose degrees of freedom count the cells that are free to vary.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Earlier tests in this chapter handled quantitative or ordinal outcomes. Here the data are counts of people in categories. For each cell, O − E is how far reality departs from the null hypothesis. A count behaves roughly like a Poisson variable, whose variance equals its mean (recall §5.7.1.3), so √E is roughly its SD and (O − E) ÷ √E is roughly a standardised deviation, like a z-score. Squaring and adding these gives a sum of approximately squared standard Normals: exactly the recipe for a χ² variable. That is the whole logic. It is not a partition of variance, which is ANOVA’s logic (recall §9.5.1).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In the CBHI survey, is membership (member or not) associated with maternal education? §10.6.1 works out the expected counts and X² for this 3 × 2 table.

points.html: Two uses: the test of independence between two categorical variables (§10.6.1) and the goodness-of-fit test of one variable against hypothesised proportions (§10.6.2).

The χ² distribution is only an approximation for counts. Its validity depends on the expected counts, not the sample size as such (§10.6.1). When the expected counts are too small, use an exact test (§10.7).
X² tests whether there is an association. It does not measure how strong it is; for a 2 × 2 table, §10.6.4 gives the measures.

blocks.html: Chi-Square Test of Independence

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The chi-square test of independence tests H₀: two categorical variables are independent (recall §5.4), against H₁: they are associated. In a table with r rows and c columns, the expected count in row i, column j is

Eᵢⱼ = (row i total × column j total) ÷ N,

and X² is referred to the χ² distribution with (r − 1)(c − 1) degrees of freedom.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: If membership had nothing to do with education, the 30% overall membership rate would hold in every education group. So the expected number of members among the 168 households with no maternal education is 30% of 168 = 50.4. That is the formula: (168 × 150) ÷ 500.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Expected counts. Under independence, P(row i and column j) = P(row i) × P(column j) (recall §5.4). Estimate each probability by its margin: (row total ÷ N) × (column total ÷ N). Multiply by N to turn it into a count: Eᵢⱼ = row total × column total ÷ N.

Degrees of freedom. The expected counts are built from the margins, so X² asks how the counts are arranged given the row and column totals. Count the cells you can fill freely once the totals are fixed:

  1. In a 2 × 2 table with fixed totals, choose the top-left count a. Then b = row 1 total − a, c = column 1 total − a, and d = row 2 total − c. One free cell: df = 1.
  2. In an r × c table, fill the first r − 1 rows and c − 1 columns freely. The last column in each row is set by the row totals, and the last row by the column totals. Free cells: (r − 1)(c − 1).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
CBHI membership by maternal education (500 households):

Maternal education Member Non-member Total
None 31 (E 50.4) 137 (E 117.6) 168
Primary 50 (E 53.1) 127 (E 123.9) 177
Secondary+ 69 (E 46.5) 86 (E 108.5) 155
Total 150 350 500

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Expected counts, e.g. none/member: 168 × 150 ÷ 500 = 50.4; secondary+/member: 155 × 150 ÷ 500 = 46.5. The others are in the table.
  2. Cell contributions (O − E)²/E. Members: (31 − 50.4)²/50.4 = 7.467; (50 − 53.1)²/53.1 = 0.181; (69 − 46.5)²/46.5 = 10.887. Non-members: 3.200; 0.078; 4.666.
  3. X² = 7.467 + 0.181 + 10.887 + 3.200 + 0.078 + 4.666 = 26.48.
  4. df = (3 − 1)(2 − 1) = 2. The 5% critical value is 5.99; p = 1.8 × 10⁻⁶.
  5. Reading the contributions: most of X² comes from the extremes of education, with fewer members than expected among mothers with no schooling and more among secondary+.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cb  <- read.csv("data/cbhi_survey.csv")
edu <- factor(cb$maternal_education,
              levels = c("none", "primary", "secondary+"))
tab <- table(edu, member = cb$cbhi_member)
res <- chisq.test(tab)
round(res$expected, 1)
res
            member
edu              0    1
  none       117.6 50.4
  primary    123.9 53.1
  secondary+ 108.5 46.5

    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  tab
X-squared = 26.479, df = 2, p-value = 1.779e-06

res$expected reproduces step 1; X-squared, df and p are steps 3 and 4. (R applies Yates’ correction, §10.6.3, only to 2 × 2 tables.)

points.html: When is the approximation adequate? A widely used convention, traced to Cochran (1954) (Rayson et al., 2004), is that no more than 20% of cells should have an expected count below 5 and no cell an expected count below 1 (Kim, 2017). For a 2 × 2 table this is usually read as all four expected counts ≥ 5. It is a rule of thumb, not a theorem, and it concerns expected counts: a small observed count, even zero, is not by itself a problem. Here the smallest expected count is 46.5, so the rule is met easily.
When the rule fails: use an exact test (Fisher’s, §10.7), or merge adjacent categories if the merged categories still make sense. Yates’ correction (§10.6.3) is not a remedy.

A significant X² shows association, not causation or direction. Education is itself linked to wealth and distance, so this association may partly reflect those other factors (confounding, the subject of §11.6).

blocks.html: Chi-Square Goodness of Fit

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The chi-square goodness-of-fit test asks whether the counts of a single categorical variable match a hypothesised set of proportions. The expected count in category i is Eᵢ = N × pᵢ, where pᵢ is the hypothesised proportion, and X² = Σ(O − E)²/E has k − 1 degrees of freedom for k categories.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: There is only one variable, so the expected counts come from the hypothesis, not from row and column totals. Once N is fixed, the first k − 1 counts determine the last, so df = k − 1. If you also estimate parameters from the data to set the pᵢ, you lose one further df for each one.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A PHC recorded 500 deliveries in a year: 140, 110, 115 and 135 in the four quarters. Is there a seasonal pattern, or are deliveries spread evenly? Treating the quarters as equal in length, H₀ gives pᵢ = 0.25 in each.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. E = 500 × 0.25 = 125 in each quarter.
  2. (O − E)²/E: (15)²/125 = 1.8; (−15)²/125 = 1.8; (−10)²/125 = 0.8; (10)²/125 = 0.8.
  3. X² = 1.8 + 1.8 + 0.8 + 0.8 = 5.2, df = 4 − 1 = 3.
  4. The 5% critical value with 3 df is 7.81; p = 0.16. These data do not show clear seasonality.

points.html: Expected counts come from the hypothesis times N; df = k − 1 (minus one more for each parameter estimated from the data).

A common use is to check a sample’s make-up against known population proportions (by age group, sex or residence from the Census, recall §1.4.4). A clear misfit warns that the sample is unrepresentative, which biases descriptive estimates (recall §6.4) and may limit generalisability (§17.1.2: external validity).
A non-significant result does not prove the hypothesised distribution is right; it shows only that these data cannot rule it out (recall §8.5).

blocks.html: Yates’ Correction

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Yates’ continuity correction modifies Pearson’s X² for a 2 × 2 table by reducing each absolute difference |O − E| by 0.5 before squaring:

X²_Yates = Σ (|O − E| − 0.5)² ÷ E.

It is the 2 × 2 version of the continuity correction for approximating a discrete count by a continuous curve (recall §5.7.2.2.4).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Counts move in whole steps, but the χ² curve is smooth. Pearson’s X² tends to give p-values a little smaller than the exact ones in small 2 × 2 tables. Shrinking each gap by half a count makes X² smaller and p larger. The correction often overshoots, making the test conservative (p too large); the small pilot table in §10.7 (Fisher’s exact test, an exact calculation for small tables) shows both errors side by side. It does not rescue a table whose expected counts are too small: that problem is solved only by an exact test (§10.7).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Recall the infant cohort of §8.7: 200 infants were followed from birth; 80 were not exclusively breastfed (not EBF) and 120 were. Diarrhoea during follow-up:

Diarrhoea No diarrhoea Total
Not EBF a = 33 b = 47 80
EBF c = 14 d = 106 120
Total 47 153 200

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
The uncorrected test on this table was worked cell by cell in §9.1.2 (step 5): expected counts 18.8, 61.2, 28.2 and 91.8, all ≥ 5; |O − E| = 14.2 in every cell (in a 2 × 2 table this is always so: with one free cell, every cell is off by the same amount); Pearson X² = 23.37 = 4.83², df = 1, p = 1.3 × 10⁻⁶. Now add Yates’ correction.

  1. Shortcut formula for Pearson’s X², same answer: X² = N(ad − bc)² ÷ [(a + b)(c + d)(a + c)(b + d)] = 200 × (3,498 − 658)² ÷ (80 × 120 × 47 × 153) = 200 × 2,840² ÷ 69,033,600 = 23.37.
  2. Yates: (14.2 − 0.5)² = 13.7² = 187.69, so X²_Yates = 187.69 × (1/18.8 + 1/61.2 + 1/28.2 + 1/91.8) = 21.75, p = 3.1 × 10⁻⁶. The shortcut form is N(|ad − bc| − N/2)² ÷ [(a + b)(c + d)(a + c)(b + d)] = 200 × 2,740² ÷ 69,033,600 = 21.75.
  3. Both far exceed 3.84, the 5% point of χ² with 1 df. With expected counts this large, the correction barely matters.

tb

The table is the one above; the two statistics are Pearson’s 23.37 (§9.1.2) and the Yates-corrected 21.75 of step 2. Note that R applies Yates by default to every 2 × 2 table, so state which version you report.

points.html: Yates’ correction applies only to 2 × 2 tables and makes X² smaller (when |O − E| is below 0.5, only |O − E| is subtracted, as R does, so the correction never increases X²).
It is a continuity correction, not a small-sample fix. When expected counts are below the Cochran threshold, use Fisher’s exact test (§10.7), not a corrected X².
Report which version you used; the two can straddle 0.05 when the result is borderline.

questions.prompt: A 2 × 3 table has 500 observations. How many degrees of freedom does the test of independence have, and why, in terms of free cells?
questions.answer: df = (2 − 1)(3 − 1) = 2. With the row and column totals fixed, you can fill in only the first two cells of the first row freely. The third cell of that row is fixed by the row total, and every cell of the second row is fixed by the column totals.

questions.prompt: In a 2 × 2 table, a = 20, b = 30, c = 10, d = 40. Compute the expected count for cell a and the Pearson X². Is it significant at 5%?
questions.answer: Row totals 50 and 50; column totals 30 and 70; N = 100. E_a = 50 × 30 ÷ 100 = 15. X² = N(ad − bc)² ÷ [(a + b)(c + d)(a + c)(b + d)] = 100 × (800 − 300)² ÷ (50 × 50 × 30 × 70) = 25,000,000 ÷ 5,250,000 = 4.76. This exceeds 3.84 (the 5% point with 1 df); p = 0.029, so it is significant at 5%. (Check by cells: |O − E| = 5 in every cell; 25/15 + 25/35 + 25/15 + 25/35 = 4.76.)

questions.prompt: “My 2 × 2 table has an expected count of 2.1, so I applied Yates’ correction.” What is wrong with this?
questions.answer: Yates’ correction is a continuity correction for approximating discrete counts with the continuous χ² curve. It does not make the χ² approximation valid when expected counts are too small. With an expected count of 2.1, one cell in four (25%) is below 5, which breaks Cochran’s convention for a 2 × 2 table. The right analysis is Fisher’s exact test (§10.7).

blocks.html: Risk, Odds and Measures of Association and Impact in the 2 × 2 Table

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Lay out a 2 × 2 table with exposure in rows and outcome in columns: a = exposed with outcome, b = exposed without, c = unexposed with outcome, d = unexposed without.

  • Risk in each group (cohort data only): R₁ = a/(a + b) in the exposed, R₀ = c/(c + d) in the unexposed (recall risk, §1.5).
  • Risk ratio (RR) = R₁/R₀. Risk difference (RD) = R₁ − R₀, also called the attributable risk (AR).
  • Odds of the outcome (recall §5.5.3): a/b in the exposed, c/d in the unexposed. Odds ratio (OR) = (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = ad/bc.
  • Attributable fraction in the exposed (AR%) = (R₁ − R₀)/R₁ = (RR − 1)/RR.
  • Population attributable risk (PAR) = R_t − R₀, where R_t is the risk in the whole population. Population attributable fraction (PAF) = PAR/R_t. With pₑ the proportion of the population exposed, Levin’s formula is PAF = pₑ(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + pₑ(RR − 1)] (Levin, 1953).
  • Number needed to treat (NNT) = 1/|RD| for a beneficial exposure; for a harmful one it is the number needed to harm (NNH) (Laupacis et al., 1988).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
The χ² test (§10.6.1) asks only whether there is an association. These measures say how strong it is and how much disease it accounts for. Ratios (RR, OR) describe strength: how many times more likely. Differences (RD, NNT) describe absolute impact: how many extra cases per 100 exposed. The PAF asks what share of all cases in the population would not occur if the exposure were removed, which depends both on the RR and on how common the exposure is.

Which measures a table can give depends on the design (recall §1.5). A cohort samples on exposure and follows people, so the row totals are real groups at risk and R₁, R₀, RR and RD are all valid. A case-control study samples on outcome: the investigator fixes the column totals (how many cases, how many controls). The rows no longer contain a population at risk, so risks, RR and RD cannot be computed. Only the OR survives, and it survives exactly (derivation below). A cross-sectional survey gives prevalences and their ratio (§13.7 estimates prevalence ratios directly).

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
The OR survives case-control sampling. Suppose a case-control study takes all cases but only a fraction f of the non-cases. The table becomes a, fb, c, fd. The OR is a(fd) ÷ (fb × c) = ad/bc, unchanged. The “risk” a/(a + fb), by contrast, depends on f, which the investigator chose.

The exposure OR equals the disease OR. A case-control study compares the odds of exposure in cases (a/c) with that in controls (b/d): (a/c) ÷ (b/d) = ad/bc. This is the same number as the odds ratio of disease, so a case-control study estimates the cohort’s OR.

When OR ≈ RR. OR = RR × (1 − R₀)/(1 − R₁). When the outcome is rare in both groups, both brackets are near 1 and OR ≈ RR. When it is common, the OR lies further from 1 than the RR.

Levin’s formula. The population risk is a weighted average: R_t = pₑR₁ + (1 − pₑ)R₀ = R₀[1 + pₑ(RR − 1)]. So PAF = (R_t − R₀)/R_t = pₑ(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + pₑ(RR − 1)].

Standard errors on the log scale. Ratios are skewed (they cannot go below 0 but can go far above 1), so their CIs are built for ln RR and ln OR and then exponentiated back.

  1. A small change in p changes ln p by about (change in p) ÷ p. So Var(ln p̂) ≈ Var(p̂)/p² = [p(1 − p)/n]/p² = 1/(np) − 1/n, estimated by 1/a − 1/(a + b) for R₁.
  2. The two groups are independent, so variances add: SE(ln RR) = √[1/a − 1/(a + b) + 1/c − 1/(c + d)].
  3. Similarly, a small change in p changes ln[p/(1 − p)] by about (change in p) ÷ [p(1 − p)], so Var(ln odds) ≈ 1/(np) + 1/(n(1 − p)), estimated by 1/a + 1/b. Adding both groups gives Woolf’s formula SE(ln OR) = √(1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/d) (Woolf, 1955).
  4. 95% CI: exp(ln estimate ± 1.96 × SE) (recall §7.2).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: The EBF cohort from §10.6.3: 80 infants not exclusively breastfed, 33 with diarrhoea; 120 exclusively breastfed, 14 with diarrhoea. Here “exposure” is not being exclusively breastfed.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Risks: R₁ = 33/80 = 0.412; R₀ = 14/120 = 0.117.
  2. RR = 0.4125/0.1167 = 3.54. Not-EBF infants had 3.5 times the risk of diarrhoea during follow-up.
  3. SE(ln RR) = √(1/33 − 1/80 + 1/14 − 1/120) = √0.0809 = 0.284. ln RR = 1.263. CI: exp(1.263 ± 1.96 × 0.284) = exp(0.705) to exp(1.820) = 2.02 to 6.17.
  4. Odds: 33/47 = 0.702 and 14/106 = 0.132. OR = (33 × 106)/(47 × 14) = 3,498/658 = 5.32.
  5. SE(ln OR) = √(1/33 + 1/47 + 1/14 + 1/106) = √0.1324 = 0.364. ln OR = 1.671. CI: exp(1.671 ± 0.713) = 2.61 to 10.85.
  6. OR (5.32) is well above RR (3.54) because diarrhoea is common here (23.5% overall): 3.54 × (1 − 0.117)/(1 − 0.412) = 3.54 × 1.503 = 5.32.
  7. RD (attributable risk) = 0.4125 − 0.1167 = 0.296: 29.6 extra infants with diarrhoea per 100 not exclusively breastfed. SE(RD) = √(0.4125 × 0.5875/80 + 0.1167 × 0.8833/120) = 0.062, so 95% CI 0.174 to 0.418 (recall §7.2.3).
  8. NNH = 1/0.296 = 3.4: for about every 3 to 4 infants not exclusively breastfed, one extra has diarrhoea (95% CI 2.4 to 5.8, the reciprocals of the RD limits). Read the other way, if the association were causal, about 3 to 4 infants would need to be exclusively breastfed to prevent one case.
  9. AR% = (3.54 − 1)/3.54 = 71.7%: of the diarrhoea cases among not-EBF infants, about 72% would be attributable to not being exclusively breastfed, if the association is causal.
  10. pₑ = 80/200 = 0.40; R_t = 47/200 = 0.235. PAR = 0.235 − 0.117 = 0.118. PAF = 0.118/0.235 = 50.4%, and Levin’s formula gives the same: 0.40 × 2.54 ÷ (1 + 0.40 × 2.54) = 1.014 ÷ 2.014 = 50.4%.
  11. Case-control check: keep all 47 cases but only half the 153 controls (f = 0.5, so 23.5 and 53 on average). The OR is 33 × 53 ÷ (23.5 × 14) = 5.32, unchanged, but the “risk” in the exposed becomes 33/56.5 = 0.58 instead of 0.41, which is meaningless.

epi.2by2 expects the exposed row first and the outcome-present column first, which is why the factor levels are set to 1:0. Each line matches a step: risks per 100 (step 1), RR and OR with the log-scale CIs (steps 3 and 5), attributable risk 29.58 per 100 (step 7), AR% (step 9), PAR 11.83 per 100 and PAF 50.35% (step 10), and Pearson’s X² (§10.6.3). epitools::riskratio() and epitools::oddsratio() give the same RR and OR one at a time.

points.html: Cohort → risk, RR, RD, NNT, AR%, PAF. Case-control → OR only (it estimates the cohort OR). Cross-sectional → prevalence, prevalence ratio or prevalence OR.
The OR is not a risk ratio. It approximates the RR only when the outcome is rare; with a common outcome, calling an OR of 5.32 “five times the risk” exaggerates a real RR of 3.54.
The null value of a ratio is 1 and of a difference is 0. A CI for RR or OR is asymmetric on the ordinary scale because it is symmetric on the log scale.

AR%, PAF and NNT assume the association is causal and unconfounded. They are statements about what removing the exposure would do. The EBF result has not yet been checked for confounding by PHC (§11.7 does this).
PAF needs pₑ from the population. Using the cohort’s 40% assumes the cohort is representative.
A quick link to the χ² test: a test-based SE is ln OR ÷ √X² = 1.671 ÷ 4.83 = 0.346, which gives a CI of 2.70 to 10.47, close to Woolf’s. Both tests address the same H₀ (OR = 1).

blocks.html: Chi-Square Test for Trend

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
When the rows of a 2-column table are ordered categories (education level, wealth quintile, age group), the chi-square test for trend (the Cochran–Armitage test) tests whether the proportion with the outcome rises or falls steadily across the ordered categories. Give each category a score sᵢ (usually 0, 1, 2, …). With xᵢ outcomes out of nᵢ in category i, p̄ = Σxᵢ/N and s̄ = Σnᵢsᵢ/N:

T = Σxᵢsᵢ − p̄Σnᵢsᵢ, V = p̄(1 − p̄)[Σnᵢsᵢ² − (Σnᵢsᵢ)²/N], X²_trend = T²/V, on 1 df.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The ordinary r × 2 test (§10.6.1) asks whether the proportions differ in any way, and spends r − 1 df to do it. If you expect a steady gradient, put all the evidence into one question, “is there a slope?”, which costs only 1 df. The test fits a straight line through the proportions (weighted by group size) and asks whether its slope differs from zero (Armitage, 1955). What is left, X²(total) − X²_trend on r − 2 df, tests departure from linear trend.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
1. Because p̄Σnᵢsᵢ = Σxᵢ × s̄, T = Σxᵢ(sᵢ − s̄): it compares the scores of the people with the outcome with the average score.
  2. Treat each person’s outcome as 0 or 1 and fit a straight line of outcome on score. Its slope is b = T ÷ S_ss, with S_ss = Σnᵢ(sᵢ − s̄)² = Σnᵢsᵢ² − (Σnᵢsᵢ)²/N (the least-squares slope, a formula derived in Chapter 12).
  3. Under H₀ (no trend) each outcome has variance p̄(1 − p̄) (recall §5.7.1.1), so Var(T) = p̄(1 − p̄)S_ss = V.
  4. T ÷ √V is approximately standard Normal, so X²_trend = T²/V is approximately χ² with 1 df (recall §5.7.2.4).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: The CBHI membership table from §10.6.1: members were 31/168 (18.5%) with no maternal education, 50/177 (28.2%) with primary and 69/155 (44.5%) with secondary or higher. Scores 0, 1, 2.

blocks.alt: Bar chart of CBHI membership proportion by maternal education with a fitted straight line
blocks.caption: Figure 10.2. CBHI membership by maternal education (500 households). The line is the fitted linear trend, rising 0.130 per education level; the bars sit close to it, so there is little departure from linearity.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. p̄ = 150/500 = 0.30. Σxᵢsᵢ = 0 × 31 + 1 × 50 + 2 × 69 = 188. Σnᵢsᵢ = 0 × 168 + 177 + 2 × 155 = 487. Σnᵢsᵢ² = 177 + 4 × 155 = 797.
  2. T = 188 − 0.30 × 487 = 188 − 146.1 = 41.9.
  3. S_ss = 797 − 487²/500 = 797 − 474.34 = 322.66. V = 0.30 × 0.70 × 322.66 = 67.76.
  4. X²_trend = 41.9² ÷ 67.76 = 1,755.6 ÷ 67.76 = 25.91, 1 df, p = 3.6 × 10⁻⁷.
  5. Slope b = 41.9 ÷ 322.66 = 0.130: membership rises by about 13 percentage points per education level.
  6. Departure from trend: 26.48 − 25.91 = 0.57 on 3 − 2 = 1 df, p = 0.45. The rise is well described by a straight line.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cb  <- read.csv("data/cbhi_survey.csv")

points.html: Use it when categories are ordered and a gradient is the question (a dose–response pattern). It is more powerful than the r × c test against a steady trend, and blind to a U-shape.
The result depends on the scores chosen. Equally spaced scores assume equal steps between levels; state your scores.
A significant trend is an association. Here education travels with wealth and distance, so the gradient is not yet an effect of education (§11.6). §12.4.5 extends trend tests to regression models.

questions.prompt: In a cohort, 30 of 100 smokers and 10 of 100 non-smokers develop a cough. Compute RR, OR, RD and NNH. Why do RR and OR differ?
questions.answer: R₁ = 0.30, R₀ = 0.10. RR = 0.30/0.10 = 3.0. OR = (30 × 90)/(70 × 10) = 2,700/700 = 3.86. RD = 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.20 (20 extra coughs per 100 smokers). NNH = 1/0.20 = 5. The OR is further from 1 because the outcome is common: OR = RR × (1 − R₀)/(1 − R₁) = 3 × 0.90/0.70 = 3.86. The two agree only when the outcome is rare in both groups.

questions.prompt: Why can a case-control study not estimate the risk ratio directly, although it can estimate the odds ratio?
questions.answer: The investigator chooses how many cases and controls to include, so the proportion of cases in each exposure row reflects that choice, not a risk in a population at risk. Sampling a fraction f of non-cases multiplies b and d by f, which changes a/(a + b) but leaves ad/bc unchanged. Also, the odds ratio of exposure (cases vs controls) equals the odds ratio of disease (exposed vs unexposed), so the case-control OR estimates the same quantity a cohort would.

questions.prompt: Using Levin’s formula, find the PAF when 20% of the population is exposed and RR = 3.
questions.answer: PAF = pₑ(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + pₑ(RR − 1)] = 0.20 × 2 ÷ (1 + 0.20 × 2) = 0.40 ÷ 1.40 = 0.286, or 28.6%, assuming the association is causal and unconfounded.
